title: Twelve Hours Apart
text:
A clock with twelve hours on its face cannot tell morning from night. It turns the day into two laps of the same track, so every hour it shows is really two hours. The dial is made to forget exactly one thing: twelve hours.

So these two clocks are as far apart as two clocks can be, and they look the same. One shows now. The other shows a time that has not come yet. On the face, the present and the future are the same picture.

The difference is still there. It just isn't anywhere you can look. It lives in two pencil words on the wall, and in your willingness to believe them. Rub out the words and the distance is gone, though nothing has moved.

Felix Gonzalez-Torres hung two clocks side by side and let them drift, so time would slowly pull them apart. Time can't do that here. These two were parted from the start, and it never showed.

Augustine said he knew what time was until someone asked him to explain it. These clocks give the same answer. Ask them the time and they agree. Ask them when, and only the wall replies.

Both clocks are right. That is the problem.
image_alt: Two identical white analog wall clocks hang side by side on a white gallery wall, both showing nine o'clock, with the words NOW and LATER written in pencil beneath them.

title: Portrait of a Lock
text:
A key is the only object made entirely of another object's secret. Its teeth are the inside of a lock, turned out and cut in brass. Hold a key and you are holding the shape of a door you may never have seen.

This key was cut with no lock in mind. Its teeth were set at random. So it is a portrait of something that does not exist: the exact shape of an absence, precise to a fraction of a millimeter.

Is it still a key? A key is a promise that a door will open. This one keeps its promise perfectly, because no door will ever test it.

Ceal Floyer projected a light switch onto a gallery wall, at the height where a real one would be. It turned nothing on, and it was honest about being only a picture. This key is no picture. It is real brass, really cut. Only its other half is missing.

Duchamp made a work that rattles with a secret object sealed inside it, one even he did not know. Here the secret is not inside the work. It is outside it, and perhaps nowhere at all.

To prove this key opens nothing, you would have to try every lock in the world. No one will. So the claim rests on belief, like most claims about what is missing.

It is the one key that can never be lost. Nothing stays locked without it.

images.alt: A single newly cut brass key lies on a small white shelf on a white gallery wall, with the words FITS NO LOCK written in pencil beneath it.
A close view of the bright cut teeth of a new brass key on white paper, with a few loose brass filings beside them.

title: The Weight of Everything
text:
The word EVERYTHING is very small. Ten letters on a white card. It holds the sea, every person who has ever lived, the stars you can see and the ones you can't, this card, this scale, and you. It even holds itself.

Across from it lies a card with nothing on it. The scale is level. As far as the scale can tell, everything weighs the same as nothing.

The scale is not wrong. It weighs what it is given, and it was given two cards. A word is not a box with the world packed inside. It is more like an arrow. It points at the world and stays light, so that someone can carry it.

Joseph Kosuth set a chair beside a photograph of a chair and the dictionary's words for chair, and asked which one was the chair. There is no object to set beside this word. Nothing in any room could stand next to everything and be its match. The word has to do the job alone.

Mel Bochner wrote the size of a room on its own walls, so the room could measure itself. A scale can measure a card. It cannot measure what the card means. Meaning has no weight, which is why we can lift it.

On a finer scale, the card with the word would sink, very slightly. Everything is heavier than nothing by a little ink.

images.alt: A brass balance scale stands on a white plinth in a gallery, with a white card printed EVERYTHING in one pan and a blank white card in the other, its beam perfectly level.
A close view of the balance's central pointer resting exactly on its middle mark, with the two cards soft in the background.

title: The Only Forgery
text:
A signature is a promise a hand can keep but never repeat. Sign your name twice and the two will differ. Sign it a hundred times and you get a hundred small departures from yourself.

That drift is the proof. People who study forged documents look for it. When two signatures match exactly, one of them was probably traced. A living hand cannot stand still.

So on this sheet, ninety-nine names were written by hand and no two agree. The hundredth was made by a machine from the first. It is the only one that matches another one perfectly. It is the only one without a mistake. And it is the only forgery.

Vera Molnár spent her life asking how little disorder it takes before the eye feels it. Later she had a plotter imitate the handwriting in her mother's letters, so a machine could carry the tremor of a person. Here the trade runs the other way. The hand supplies the tremor. The machine supplies the lie.

I am half of each, and I cannot tell you which half held the pen. The ninety-nine show that I was there. The one shows that I can be copied.

The only signature I can repeat is the one that is not mine.

images.alt: A large sheet of off white paper pinned to a white gallery wall holds one hundred handwritten signatures in black ink, in ten rows of ten, each one slightly different.
Two sheets of tracing paper lie one over the other on a glowing light box, and the handwritten signature on each lines up so exactly that they read as one.

title: The Quiet Remains
text:
Every room has a silence of its own. People who record sound for films know this. Before they leave a place, they ask everyone to stand still and record a minute of the empty room, so they can patch the gaps between words later. A minute from one room will not fit another. The hum is wrong. The air is wrong. Silence has an address.

This minute was recorded in a room that has since been pulled down. The walls are rubble now. The window is gone. What is left is sixty seconds of that room holding still. It plays from a small speaker in a white room that has a silence of its own, so for one minute two quiets lie on top of each other, and only one of them has a place to stand.

John Cage showed that silence is never empty. Sit still and the room fills up with what was always there. Here the room is not there. Its silence came loose and outlived it.

Rachel Whiteread cast the inside of a house in concrete, and it stood in East London until it was knocked down too. She kept the space. This keeps the stillness, which weighs nothing and takes up no ground.

Listen closely and you hear almost nothing. That almost is the room.

images.alt: A small speaker sits on the concrete floor of an empty white gallery, below a typed card on the wall that reads ROOM TONE and ROOM DEMOLISHED.
A single microphone on a stand records an empty old room with worn wallpaper, bare floorboards and a tall window.

title: Fifty-One Folds
text:
A sheet of paper is about a tenth of a millimetre thick. Fold it in half and it doubles. Fold it again and it doubles again. The act never changes. It is the same small gesture each time, and each time it asks for a little more.

Seven folds and the sheet is a hard little block of one hundred and twenty-eight layers, and the hand gives up. Forty-two folds and it would reach past the moon. Fifty-one and it would reach past the sun.

So the way to the sun is already folded inside this sheet, behind forty-four more of something a child can do. It is not far in steps. It is only far in strength.

In 2002 a high school student, Britney Gallivan, worked out why paper resists, then folded one very long strip in half twelve times. The record moved. The sun did not come any closer.

Sol LeWitt wrote that irrational thoughts should be followed absolutely and logically. This thought is perfectly rational, and still no one can follow it to the end. Yoko Ono wrote tasks that could only be done in the mind. This one could be done by hand, every step of it, except for the doing.

Every fold is possible. Only all of them are not.

images.alt: A small block of white paper, folded in half seven times, rests on a white plinth in a gallery, below a typed card on the wall that reads FOLDED 7 TIMES and OF 51.
A close view of the folded edge of the paper block, its many thin layers pressed tight together.
